finding: Old Babylonian copy dated to Ammisaduqa year 12 (~1635 BCE)
notes: A dated written flood tradition predates the extant Genesis composition window by roughly a millennium.

finding: Old Babylonian Sumerian and Akkadian flood traditions precede Standard Babylonian Gilgamesh XI
notes: Do not date the tradition solely from the 7th-century K.3375 witness.

finding: OUP studies argue both pre-P and P Genesis flood layers were modeled on earlier Mesopotamian traditions; Day argues several features are closer to Atrahasis than Gilgamesh
notes: The exact direct/indirect route and timing remain debated; motif overlap alone is not the basis for this evidence.

finding: Cuneiform records document Judean deportee communities in Neo-Babylonian and Achaemenid Babylonia
notes: Presence in Babylonia establishes opportunity, not proof that a particular flood text was read by a Genesis author.

finding: No named intermediary manuscript/scribe connecting Atrahasis/Gilgamesh to Genesis is frozen
notes: Keep route as unresolved even though broader literary dependence is well supported in cited scholarship.

finding: Critical scholarship argues early Yu material is fundamentally water-control/cosmogonic habitability rather than a Noah-style exterminatory survival story
notes: Consistent with low survival-package Jaccard in the frozen Chinese bundle.

finding: Science 2016 proposed a massive Yellow River outburst flood as a possible basis for the Great Flood tradition
notes: This is a hypothesis about historical anchoring, not direct proof of textual origin.

finding: Later geological and historical work disputes direct identification and/or the textual-historical inference
notes: Environmental convergence remains plausible at the broad water-disaster level, but a unique event-to-myth mapping is not secure.

finding: ETCSL lines 24-37 explicitly combine clay kneading/form production with the purpose of carrying labor baskets
ORACC explicitly notes Atrahasis creates humans from clay plus slain-god blood, while Enki and Ninmah creates humans from clay
notes: Shared clay motif alone does not establish direct copying.

finding: Old Babylonian schools taught Sumerian language/literature and maintained cultural heritage in an Akkadian-speaking environment
notes: Provides a mechanism for cross-language literary continuity without identifying a direct source text.

finding: No source in the frozen evidence demonstrates direct copying between the two compositions
notes: Current conclusion is shared repertoire + transmission substrate, not a one-text genealogy.

finding: Watkins reconstructs comparative Indo-European poetic/dragon-slaying formulae across Vedic, Hittite, Greek and other traditions
effect_on_mechanism: supports ancestry hypothesis beyond raw motif count
notes: This explains why low-dimensional Jaccard is not sufficient to reject genealogical continuity.

finding: Only one shared-positive motif in current 8-feature bundle; simple matching is inflated by six shared absences
notes: Retain as methodological negative control for metric interpretation.
